title: Ignis Innovation | Clean Cooking for African Institutions
section: Why can steam use less fuel?
text:
An open fire sends a large share of its heat into the surrounding air. A centralised steam system contains combustion in an enclosed generator and transfers heat through steam to the cooking vessels. One heat source can serve several cooking points, and indirect heating delivers heat evenly through the vessel walls. More of the energy bought as fuel goes into cooking rather than being lost around the kitchen.
Enclosed, insulated generator.
One heat source for the whole kitchen.

title: What We Do: Institutional Clean Cooking
text:
An open fire wastes most of its wood. In field tests, open fires delivered on average only about 11% of the wood's energy to the pot. Even a carefully tended fire reaches only 20 to 30%. The rest escapes as heat and smoke. An enclosed, insulated system puts far more of each kilogram to work.
Enclosed, insulated steam generator.
Combustion happens in a closed firebox, so far less heat escapes than from an open fire.
One heat source for the whole kitchen.
A single generator replaces many open fires; there is no longer a separate fire idling under each pot.
Indirect heating in jacketed kettles.
Steam heats the pot walls evenly and hands over its heat as it condenses, so food cooks without scorching and heat goes into the food, not the room.
Fuel choice and control.
The generator can run on processed fuels such as briquettes or pellets, and the firing rate can be controlled to match meal times.
Operation and monitoring.
Metered, monitored systems (via CleanCookIQ) catch waste early, and cooks spend less time tending fires.
Enclosed, insulated generator.
One heat source for the whole kitchen.
Indirect heating in jacketed kettles.
Share of fuel energy reaching the pot
Open fire (field average) 11%
Open fire (well tended, lab) 20–30%
Improved institutional stove (manufacturer's claim) 62%
At 11% efficiency, a kitchen burns about nine times the wood its food actually needs; at 62%, about 1.6 times. The 62% is a manufacturer's claim for an improved institutional stove, included for comparison only.
Third-party figures, not Ignis measurements. Sources: Aprovecho Research Center (2026), citing Urban et al.: 11.3% average across 254 field tests of open fires in Malawi, Ghana and Kenya. · Low-Tech Magazine (2014): well-tended open fires reach 20–30%. · Shengzhou Stove Manufacturer (2026): 62% for an improved institutional stove. text:
Financing Financing the transition from the energy budget you already have.
Institutional clean cooking requires capital for equipment, installation and implementation. Ignis works to structure financing so that the institution's transition can be repaid over time through a service arrangement linked to the energy expenditure it already carries.
The exact structure depends on the institution, the project economics, the capital source and the programme design. Where applicable, capital may combine grants, concessional finance, results-based mechanisms or carbon-related finance. Availability and terms are assessed project by project.

title: Talk to Ignis: Request an Assessment
text:
How is the transition financed?
The equipment and installation have an upfront capital requirement. Where approved and available, Ignis can structure third-party capital, potentially including grants, concessional finance, results-based finance or carbon finance, with the institution repaying through a Clean Energy Service Agreement linked to its existing energy budget.
Who owns the equipment?
Ignis owns, operates and maintains the system for the length of the contract. If the kitchen goes down, that is our problem to fix.
What happens if it breaks during term?
Monitored uptime and a servicing contract mean we respond fast. Steam holds temperature between services, so a single fault rarely stops meals.
Can we keep our existing cooks?
Yes. We train your cooks on handover, same menus, faster, in clean air instead of smoke.
How long is the contract?
Structured around the payback from fuel savings. We size it during the assessment and share the terms up front.
Do you work outside Kenya?
Our current sites are in Kenya; the model is built to extend across the continent as the pipeline grows.

title: Electric Cooking
section: Built for the way Kenyan kitchens cook.
text:
A 6-litre pot, a 1000 W heating plate and a sealed lid. Asili cooks the everyday staples, githeri, uji, beans, rice and stews, under pressure, with the heat kept inside the pot.
Twelve one-touch programmes
Githeri, uji, rice, stews, kuku and more each have their own button, labelled in English and Kiswahili. Pick the dish and the cooker sets the time and pressure.
Sealed, locking lid
The lid locks before pressure builds, so heat and steam stay inside the pot instead of escaping into the kitchen.
Removable stainless inner pot
The cooking pot lifts out for serving and washing, and the outer body stays clean and dry.
Set it and walk away
Delay Start, Keep Warm, low or high pressure and a Less / Normal / More setting are on the panel, and the digital display counts the cook down.
Opens wide for easy cleaning
The lid swings fully open on its hinge, so the pot and seal are easy to reach after a cook.
Heating plate at the base
Lift the inner pot out and the heating plate sits at the bottom of the housing, so heat goes straight up into the pot rather than out into the room.
Detachable power cord
The cord plugs into a socket on the back of the cooker, so it unplugs for carrying, cleaning and storage. The unit runs on a standard 220 V supply.
